According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.21885v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A frontier model has been shown to edit the weights of a much smaller one. We ask whether a model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and find that it can, by its own reasoning, with no gradients and no training; we call this self-rewriting. Given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, a 27B model diagnoses its failure and edits the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in a test fixed in advance, and another session's edit also makes it significantly better. It keeps getting better: it submits an edit only when its own tests support it, each edit replacing the last, and over its first eight such sessions its accuracy only rises. Unlike test-time scaling, the gain persists in its weights and adds no cost per answer; unlike training, it needs no pre- or post-training infrastructure, only an open model and hours on one GPU. It repairs a damaged copy of itself: it locates the corrupted matrix and rewrites it with values of its own, never reading the undamaged weights; found on text math problems alone, the repair lifts the copy on six image benchmarks it never saw from 7% to 70% accuracy, 83% of the undamaged model's. And the ability emerges with scale: across four sizes of one family, the 2B model makes no edit and the 4B and 9B models break themselves; only the 27B model works on itself as a human would, comparing its hidden states on answers that finish and on answers that run out of tokens, weakening the direction that separates them. Like a human, a model need not separate training from inference; improving a language model may come to take a conversation rather than a training run.

We study three methods for constructing it: a closed-form first-order strike remapping, a new conditional-Gamma method, and a two-dimensional joint-law PDE that makes no distributional assumption and serves as the benchmark. The conditional-Gamma method is our main contribution. It conditions on the terminal underlying return, which preserves the state dependence of variance drag that a single remapped strike discards. Three one-dimensional forward PDEs under a calibrated local-volatility model give the conditional mean and variance of integrated variance, and a Gamma law matched to these moments keeps realised variance non-negative and prices the option in closed form. A shifted-Gamma variant that also matches the conditional third moment gives its clearest gains for inverse products at longer maturities, and a Gamma-mixture extension covers the full range of conditional skewness compatible with non-negative realised variance. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, LFM3 is our latest generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

Industry observers note that the payoff indicates at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two latest in-house encoders:.

It has been revealed that each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Industry observers note that reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

According to recent reports, reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a upcoming in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Industry observers note that reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Industry observers note that reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

In a recent development, for brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

Recent findings suggest that LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.22517v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Do shifts in public climate concern alter persistent financial risk and subsequently matter for real activity? We combine daily U.S. sectoral equity returns with a monthly Climate Concern Index (CCI) constructed from internet search intensity and decomposed into adverse and transition-oriented components. GARCH-MIDAS estimates reveal substantial heterogeneity: adverse climate concern raises persistent volatility in carbon-intensive Energy activities, while transition-oriented attention tends to reduce persistent volatility in regulated Utilities, with important differences across sub-sectors. We then construct a persistent-risk differential between Energy and Utilities and examine its predictive content for sectoral real activity using local projections. Innovations associated with adverse climate concern precede declines in Oil and Gas industrial production and employment over the following quarters, while comparable Utilities responses are limited. The production result is preserved when the financial predictor is reconstructed using the more closely matched Oil, Gas, Coal equity sub-sector and remains economically similar across several robustness checks. Overall, the findings establish a link between climate concern, persistent sectoral financial risk, and subsequent real-sector activity.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.21832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI systems are increasingly used to automate AI R&D, misaligned systems could sabotage research intended to improve model safety and alignment. To stress-test defenses against such sabotage, we use a human expert as a proxy saboteur on AI safety research. We conduct a red-team/blue-team game where a human researcher runs AI safety experiments from scratch and auditors try to tell which were sabotaged and how. Given access to the full research transcript and the ability to run experiments, human auditors mostly fail to distinguish sabotaged from benign research: they achieve an AUROC of 0.59, not significantly better than chance, and fully identify the specific sabotage in only 17% of cases. Despite not being allowed to run experiments, the best frontier models outperform human auditors (Fable 5.1: AUROC 0.73, 32% full identification) within noise and weaker models perform comparably. When the saboteur chooses which experiments are attacked, rather than being required to sabotage every question given, sabotage identification drops further. Our results suggest that research sabotage by expert-level agents is difficult to detect with current auditing methods and provide a new setting for studying research sabotage.

Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a newly introduced routing strategy for real-time endpoints.
  • Here’s the problem it solves: LLM applications such as chat assistants, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), and agents with long system prompts send many requests that start with the same text.
  • Sources indicate that prefix-aware routing picks an instance from the request alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a newly introduced routing strategy for real-time endpoints. It uses the cache state that the model container reports. It sends each request to an instance that already holds a long cached match for its prompt and isn’t too busy. It’s for teams that serve large language models (LLMs) with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. You turn it on in two places: add one environment variable to your model so the container reports its cache contents, and set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration. Your clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before.

Here’s the problem it solves: LLM applications such as chat assistants, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), and agents with long system prompts send many requests that start with the same text. A model keeps the work it did on a prompt in GPU memory, the KV cache, and skips that work when the same start reaches the same instance again. In part 1 of this series, we introduced prefix-aware routing for Amazon SageMaker AI, which sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. Prefix-aware routing infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone, so it can’t tell when an instance has evicted that cache.

Sources indicate that prefix-aware routing picks an instance from the request alone. It hashes the start of the request, up to the PrefixLength you configure (bytes of the InvokeEndpoint payload, or characters of the message text for the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API), and sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. It never sees what an instance actually has cached. This works well when every request starts with the same shared text, and less well in two cases:.

The cache on an instance changes over time. An instance evicts older KV cache entries when its GPU memory fills up, but the router keeps sending matching requests there as if the cache were still warm.

Sources indicate that A conversation starts out short. In a multi-turn chat, each turn adds to the history. While the request is still shorter than PrefixLength, every latest turn changes the text the router hashes, so the next turn can land on a different instance than the one that cached the earlier turns. The turns of a conversation stay on one instance only after the request grows past PrefixLength.

In this post, we explain how KV-aware routing works, when to use it, and how to enable, invoke, and verify it on single model endpoints and inference component endpoints.

KV-aware routing has three parts: the model container reports what it has cached, SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state for the endpoint, and the endpoint uses the index to choose an instance for each request.

When you turn events on with SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG, the container publishes a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts cache entries, and SageMaker AI uses these events to keep the index current. The index holds only pointers: one-way, truncated hashes of cached content, each mapped to the instance or inference component copy that holds it. It never stores prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. When a request arrives, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks up the tokens in the index. The index returns the instances or inference component copies that hold part of the prompt in their cache, and how much of it each one holds. For example, if instance A holds the cached start of a conversation, the next turn of that conversation goes to A. Because the index matches on tokens rather than a fixed number of bytes, a multi-turn history can match in full as it grows. A request that shares only part of its prompt still goes to the instance with the longest match.

Industry observers note that the endpoint then picks among these candidates by weighing how much of the prompt each one has cached against how busy it is. A candidate that is too busy is skipped, so if the instance with the longest match is busy, the request goes to the next-best one that is available. If no candidate has a useful match or all of them are busy, the request falls back to load-aware routing, as described in Routing overhead and fallbacks. You don’t configure a concurrency threshold for this, as you do with prefix-aware routing. The index also follows the fleet. When you scale in, entries for removed instances are dropped. When you scale out or an patch replaces instances, the newly introduced instances start with empty caches, so latency can be higher for a short time.

Recent findings suggest that figure 1: KV-aware routing on a SageMaker AI endpoint. The router looks up the managed cache index and forwards the request to the instance that holds the longest cached match. Each instance reports KV cache events back to the index.

It has been revealed that in Figure 1, the endpoint has three instances, A, B, and C. Each instance runs the same model in its own model container (the AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container listed in Requirements and limits) and has its own KV cache in GPU memory, so each instance holds different cached content: A holds turns 1 to 3 of conversation 1, B holds conversations 2 and 3, and C holds document 7. When turn 4 of conversation 1 arrives (step 1), the router tokenizes it and looks it up in the managed cache index (step 2). The index shows that A holds the first 6,000 of the request’s 6,200 tokens, so the router sends the request to A (step 3), and A only has to compute the remaining tokens. If A is busy, the router sends the request to the least busy instance instead (step 4). KV-aware routing needs a choice of destinations, so it is active only with at least two instances, or at least two copies of an inference component. With a single instance, every request goes to that instance and the setting has no effect.

Recent findings suggest that with this launch, SageMaker AI offers four routing strategies for real-time endpoints. You set the strategy per production variant in the RoutingConfig of your endpoint configuration.

Both strategies send requests to where their prefix is likely to be cached. They differ in how they know where that is, and in what they need from your container.

We measured KV-aware routing against random routing in two ways: a large-scale benchmark on production-sized instances, and a smaller, reproducible comparison you can follow in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.

In our benchmarks with Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on seven ml.p5.48xlarge instances, we ran 30-minute tests with 20 or 100 simulated users holding multi-turn chats and document Q&A sessions, with prompts of up to about 64,000 tokens. Compared with random routing, and with long prompts under load, KV-aware routing reduced p50 time to first token (TTFT) by up to 97 percent and increased throughput by up to 234 percent. It raised the KV cache hit rate from 3–48 percent to 80–93 percent. Long prompts gained even at lower load. The gain was smallest with short prompts, where there is less prefill to save. Results depend on your workload. To measure them for your own traffic, use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.

Before it routes a request, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks it up in the managed cache index. The lookup takes a few milliseconds for short prompts and longer for long ones, mostly for tokenization, but it stays small next to the time a cache hit saves. For text-only requests that use standard options, the tokens it computes are passed to the model, so the prompt isn’t tokenized twice.

If the lookup is slow, finds no useful match, or all matching instances are busy, the endpoint routes the request with load-aware routing, the same behavior as the LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS strategy. The request is still served, without the cache benefit. The same happens when the endpoint can’t tokenize a request, except in the two error cases described in Invoking the endpoint. These fallbacks aren’t reported in the SageMaker AI console or metrics at launch, so use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working to confirm that routing is effective for your traffic.

With very short prompts there is less prefill to save, so prefix-aware routing can be all you need.

Prefix-aware routing needs no changes to your container, but it can’t see what an instance actually holds. KV-aware routing asks the container what it holds, which makes it more precise. It pays off when there is a lot of cached context to reuse and that cache is under pressure: long prompts, high load, and instances that run short of GPU memory for the KV cache. When that happens, the container evicts the least recently used parts of the cache, including parts of shared prompts and conversation history.

For example, a support assistant runs on three instances, and each conversation begins with the same 6,000-token knowledge-base excerpt. Conversation 1 starts on instance A, which caches the excerpt. Traffic rises, A runs short of memory, and the container evicts most of that excerpt. Instance B recently served another conversation over the same excerpt and still holds its first 4,000 tokens. When the next turn of conversation 1 arrives, prefix-aware routing sends it to A again, and A recomputes the excerpt. With KV-aware routing, A’s container has already reported the eviction, so the index demonstrates that B holds the longest match, and the request goes to B, which recomputes only the remaining tokens. At low load, A wouldn’t have evicted anything, and both strategies would have sent the request to A with the cache intact.

KV-aware routing helps most when requests reuse cached context in ways a fixed-length prefix can’t capture:.

According to recent reports, multi-turn conversations: Each turn sends the full conversation history, so the cached prefix grows with every turn. KV-aware routing matches the whole cached history and keeps each conversation on the instance that holds it. This matters most for long conversations. After the managed cache index reflects an eviction, the router doesn’t keep sending the conversation to an instance that has already dropped its cache.

It has been revealed that high-throughput inference with shared context: RAG applications prepend retrieved documents, and assistants send long system prompts with every request. KV-aware routing fits when these prompts are long and instances are under memory pressure. With a stable shared prefix and moderate load, prefix-aware routing also fits. Put the shared content first and in the same order: if the same documents appear in a different order, the prompts no longer share a start, so they don’t match.

Workloads where prefix length is hard to tune: With prefix-aware routing, you choose a PrefixLength that covers your shared text without scattering requests that should stay together. KV-aware routing has no prefix length to tune, because it matches on what is actually cached.

Prefix-aware routing is a good fit, with no container changes, if your requests share a stable system prompt or document at the start, your prompts are short, or load is moderate. In these cases, instances have enough GPU memory to keep the shared text cached, so both strategies find it. Prefix-aware routing is also the choice if your container isn’t supported by KV-aware routing, because it works with any container that has prefix caching turned on. If your requests are short and interchangeable, or your model isn’t an LLM, there is little cached context to reuse, so use RANDOM or LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS.

If you aren’t sure which fits, start with prefix-aware routing, run your own traffic against a KV_AWARE endpoint, and compare time to first token, throughput, and hit rate as described in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.

Before you enable KV-aware routing, check that your container, endpoint, and requests meet these requirements:.

In a recent development, container: At launch, KV-aware routing supports the AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container for SageMaker AI: images with vLLM 0.33.0 or later, or the Amazon Linux build server-sagemaker-cuda-v2.8.0 or later. Prefix caching must be on, which is the default, and KV cache events must be turned on with the SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG environment variable, as shown in How to enable it. SageMaker AI doesn’t set it for you.

Endpoints and instances: Real-time single model endpoints and inference component endpoints, including dynamic Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters, on GPU instance types. You can also configure KV-aware routing with AWS CloudFormation. Routing is active only with at least two instances for a single model endpoint, or at least two copies of an inference component, which can be on the same instance. With fewer, you can still set KV_AWARE and the endpoint isn’t rejected, but every request goes to the single instance or copy.

According to recent reports, requests: OpenAI-compatible Completions or Chat Completions payloads, sent with InvokeEndpoint, InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream, or the SageMaker AI OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream isn’t supported. If you set the model field, it must match the value of SM_VLLM_MODEL.

SDK versions: Detailed observability, which you use to track the KV cache hit rate, needs AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) version 2.35.6 or later, or Boto3 version 1.43.31 or later.

SageMaker AI checks these requirements before your endpoint serves traffic. If a check fails, the request or deployment fails with a message that describes what is missing. For the full list of settings, validation behavior, and quotas, see the SageMaker AI documentation.

It has been revealed that you turn on KV-aware routing in two places: the model and the endpoint configuration. The example notebook runs every step end to end, for both a single model endpoint and an inference component endpoint.

Industry observers note that 1. Turn on KV cache events in the model – When you create the model, add SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG to the container environment. Without it, the endpoint has no cache state to route on. The ports in this setting are used only inside the instance, so you don’t open them to your network.

2. Choose KV-aware routing in the endpoint configuration – Set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the RoutingConfig of the production variant:.

If your container image is built for CUDA 13, also set InferenceAmiVersion in the production variant to an AMI that supports it, such as al2023-ami-sagemaker-inference-gpu-4-1. Otherwise the container can fail to start. See Inference GPU drivers.

Check that your account has enough endpoint quota for the instance type and count you choose, and request an increase in Service Quotas if needed.

The same RoutingConfig setting works for inference component endpoints, including dynamic LoRA adapters. For adapters, KV-aware routing chooses among the instances that already have the adapter loaded.

Nothing changes in how you call the endpoint. Send a Chat Completions payload with InvokeEndpoint, or with InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream and "stream": true in the request body:.

Industry observers note that you can also call the endpoint with the OpenAI Python client through the SageMaker AI OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. The Use the OpenAI-compatible API with SageMaker AI notebook on GitHub demonstrates how, for both single model endpoints and inference components.

In a recent development, KV-aware routing doesn’t apply the multi-tenant prefix isolation from part 1: it ignores the prefix-aware ID header and the prompt_cache_key field. A request that sets a top-level cache_salt field to a non-null value is rejected with a 400 error.

KV-aware routing adds two error cases: a request whose model field names a model that the container doesn’t serve fails with a ModelError, and a request with a non-null cache_salt is rejected with a 400 error. Errors from inference itself are returned as before, and your model container’s own logs in Amazon CloudWatch can help you find the cause. The endpoint doesn’t deliver logs about its KV-aware routing decisions to your account, so use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working, such as cached_tokens per request and the KV cache hit rate, to see how routing behaves.

In a recent development, KV-aware routing doesn’t add metrics of its own, so you check its effect on your model. There are three ways to do this.

According to recent reports, check cache hits per request – The container doesn’t report prompt token details by default, so set SM_VLLM_ENABLE_PROMPT_TOKENS_DETAILS to true in the model environment. Each response then includes usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens, the number of prompt tokens that were served from the KV cache. When you send a follow-up turn, or another request that starts the same way as an earlier one, a non-zero value reveals that the request reached an instance that held its prefix.

Check model metrics in Amazon CloudWatch – Turn on detailed observability by adding --metrics-config '{"EnableDetailedObservability": true}' when you create the endpoint configuration, using the SDK versions in Requirements and limits. SageMaker AI then publishes the model container’s metrics, including the KV cache hit rate and TTFT. Query them as described in Detailed observability with PromQL.

Figure 2: Verifying KV-aware routing. (a) A follow-up request highlights most prompt tokens served from the KV cache. (b) The KV cache hit rate for the same endpoint in the SageMaker AI Insights dashboard.

Industry observers note that compare with the strategy you would otherwise use – For most LLM workloads the real choice is between KV_AWARE and PREFIX_AWARE, so compare those two, and add a RANDOM endpoint as a baseline. Use the same model, instance type, and instance count for each endpoint, and send the same prompts at the same concurrency for the same duration, so that the only difference is the routing strategy. Make sure your test reuses context the way your production traffic does, for example with multi-turn conversations or shared documents. If KV_AWARE and PREFIX_AWARE perform about the same for your traffic, prefix-aware routing is the simpler choice.

It has been revealed that as an example of this comparison, we compared RANDOM and KV_AWARE on a small endpoint. We sent the same multi-turn workload to two endpoints that differ only in routing strategy. Each endpoint had two ml.g5.xlarge instances serving Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on a supported container. Each run sent 128 requests: 32 simulated users, each asking 4 questions about a document chosen from 12 documents of about 7,400 tokens. Each question resends the conversation so far, so every question after the first can reuse cached context. We ran two pairs of runs, with RANDOM first in pair 1 and KV_AWARE first in pair 2, and used new documents for each pair so that both endpoints started with empty caches. Table 1 indicates the results as pair 1 / pair 2.

Table 1: RANDOM and KV_AWARE routing under the same workload. Each cell shows pair 1 / pair 2. ModelLatency and OverheadLatency are Amazon CloudWatch metrics for the endpoint. The client measured time to first token and run duration. The cache share is the sum of cached_tokens divided by the sum of prompt_tokens over a run.

In a recent development, in both pairs, KV_AWARE had lower CloudWatch ModelLatency (average 1,235 and 1,314 ms against 4,124 and 5,100 ms) and lower time to first token for questions 2–4 (p50 237 and 245 ms against 1,284 and 1,632 ms). Its cache share was higher, at 90 percent in both pairs against 76 and 70 percent. OverheadLatency, the time SageMaker AI spends outside the model container, was 14 to 19 ms higher on average with KV_AWARE. This is one model, one instance type, and one workload with long shared documents, so measure your own traffic as described earlier in this section. Figure 3 shows the model latency charts that the SageMaker AI console displays for the two endpoints.

Industry observers note that figure 3: One-minute average model latency in Amazon CloudWatch for the RANDOM endpoint (blue) and the KV_AWARE endpoint (orange), on a shared 0–7 second axis. Each endpoint received seven consecutive runs of the same workload on fresh documents, RANDOM first. Average model latency was 4.9–6.2 seconds for RANDOM and 1.2–1.3 seconds for KV_AWARE. The last RANDOM point is lower because that minute holds only the last 20 requests of the run.

If neither does better than RANDOM, check that prefix caching and KV cache events are turned on in the container, as described in Requirements and limits.

The example notebook applies the steps in this post to Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on two ml.g5.xlarge instances, the minimum for a single model endpoint, and on an inference component endpoint with two copies. It calls the endpoint with both APIs, indicates in the container logs that follow-up requests are served from the KV cache, and doesn’t compare routing strategies. Run its cleanup cells at the end to avoid ongoing charges.

According to recent reports, to avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created. For an inference component endpoint, delete the inference components first (delete-inference-component), then the endpoint, endpoint configuration, and model (delete-endpoint, delete-endpoint-config, delete-model).

These three practices help you keep KV-aware routing effective after you turn it on.

Monitor the KV cache hit rate – Keep detailed observability on after launch and watch the KV cache hit rate over time in the SageMaker AI Insights dashboard (Figure 2b), or query it with PromQL, as described in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.

Industry observers note that blueprint for cold starts – The first request with newly introduced context, such as a new document or the first turn of a conversation, has nothing cached on any instance. KV-aware routing speeds up the requests that follow, not the first one.

Proposal for cache rebuilds during scaling and updates – As described in How KV-aware routing works, newly introduced instances start with empty caches. To soften the latency increase, use a rolling or blue/green update for single model endpoints, or a RollingUpdatePolicy for inference components.

KV-aware routing gives SageMaker AI real-time endpoints a second way to send requests to where their prompts are cached. It uses the cache state that your model container reports, so it follows the cache when instances evict it under memory pressure. Prefix-aware routing from part 1 of this series remains the simpler choice for stable shared prompts, short contexts, and moderate load. SageMaker AI handles routing inside the endpoint for both strategies, so you don’t build or run a routing layer yourself. You turn it on with one environment variable in the model and "RoutingStrategy": "KV_AWARE" in the endpoint configuration.

KV-aware routing is available today in all commercial AWS Regions that support SageMaker AI real-time inference, for endpoints that use a supported container. It is available at no additional charge. SageMaker AI runs and manages the cache index for you, and you pay only for the instances your endpoint uses. KV_AWARE is a latest value for the existing RoutingStrategy field, so you don’t need a new configuration object, and older versions of the AWS CLI and Boto3 accept it. To get started, read the documentation, run the example notebook on a small endpoint, and then compare KV_AWARE with PREFIX_AWARE on a copy of your own traffic.

#1335. Tech Report: Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2063 w)
📖 Baca

Tech Report: Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that language models can do a lot.
  • Industry observers note that say a customer calls your support line.
  • In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Industry observers note that say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

In a recent development, it's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Industry observers note that parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

According to recent reports, qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

Industry observers note that qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

Recent findings suggest that each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

It has been revealed that when you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who stated what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

In a recent development, the diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

In a recent development, parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

According to recent reports, what's newly introduced is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Industry observers note that apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

In a recent development, if you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

In a recent development, emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

Industry observers note that the app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

Recent findings suggest that the session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

Recent findings suggest that you use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Sources indicate that raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Recent findings suggest that like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Industry observers note that both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

In a recent development, each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Sources indicate that try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (269 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.21827v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Deep networks score near 99% on the MSTAR vehicle benchmark, and the newer ATRNet-STAR benchmark was built to be harder. We ask how much of these scores comes from the vehicle itself. With a modern network (ConvNeXt-Small, 3 seeds) we first reproduce the known MSTAR result: with the central 96x96 pixels zeroed out, accuracy is still 73.3% (chance 10%). The same shortcut is present in ATRNet-STAR, which was collected across several scenes: with the vehicle removed, accuracy is 63.3% on the 40-class SOC split (chance 2.5%). Under the official scene-change split, the background stops helping and starts hurting. Accuracy is 22.8% on full chips and 30.8% when only the vehicle is shown. A SAR foundation model, SARATR-X, leans on the background more than ConvNeXt does (+4 to +6 points with the vehicle removed, in every seed) and does not solve the scene change. We then hold the amount of training data fixed and vary the depression angles used for training. Accuracy is set mainly by the gap to the nearest training angle: 57% at 15 degrees, 39% at 30 degrees and 26% at 45 degrees. Adding more training angles does not help. Finally, when most classes have training images at the test angle and a few do not, the missing classes do worse than when no class has them: 9.0% instead of 22.4% at a 45-degree gap. Most of their images are assigned to known classes. We recommend reporting background-only and target-only controls, and the angle gap, next to any accuracy figure. Code is public.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.22277v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Can we explain asset price movements even with hindsight? Reinterpreting Roll's (1988) AFA Presidential Address, "$R^2$," as a modern empirical exercise, we show that conventional macroeconomic, cash-flow, expectations, and flow variables explain less than 10% (often with negative $R^2$) of monthly U.S. equity return variation out of sample and lack daily observations. Their content spans interpretable themes, including corporate news, macroeconomic conditions, monetary policy, sentiment, and geopolitics.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stephen Quinn joined the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in 2004 and serves as a senior computer scientist in the Information Technology Laboratory (ITL).

#1331. Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment

Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1296 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The biggest cost lever in a generative AI system is whether you call a model at all.
  • Sources indicate that the pattern usually starts in a prototype.
  • At production volume, unneeded model calls cost you in three ways:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The biggest cost lever in a generative AI system is whether you call a model at all. We often see teams route every task through a large language model (LLM), including input validation, formatting, and routing. Each call is cheap in isolation, but at production scale these small costs become one of the largest line items in the architecture. Wherever a deterministic rule can do the job, skipping the model saves money, cuts latency, and removes a source of non-determinism. In this post, you learn how to decide whether each step in a workflow needs a model at all. You can then map each option to AWS: deterministic code, a constrained decision call, or a right-sized model on Amazon Bedrock.

Sources indicate that the pattern usually starts in a prototype. A model call works for one step, so it becomes the default for the next. Those steps include validating input, reformatting a request body, and picking a route. At prototype volume, nobody notices the cost.

At production volume, unneeded model calls cost you in three ways:.

In a recent development, each newly introduced model launch then restarts the debate about which model to use. The earlier question, whether the step needs a model at all, goes unasked.

According to recent reports, cost guidance, including the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens, often starts at model selection. This post starts one step earlier: Does the step need a model at all?

Figure 1 highlights the whole decision as a flowchart with three labeled lanes: Runs as code, Questions, and Runs on a model. Take each workflow step through three questions in order, and stop at the first option that meets the step’s requirements:.

If the answer to all three is no, the step is open-ended and runs on a right-sized model.

Figure 1: Deciding whether a workflow step needs a model, and which one.

Consider a customer support assistant. The following table indicates how five of its steps go through the chart.

You can use a model when a task is open-ended, ambiguous, or generative: summarizing a document, drafting a reply, extracting meaning from prose. Use deterministic code when the task has a checkable rule: an email format, a schema, an exact keyword, a numeric range. The following table indicates what you trade away when you send a rule-shaped task to a model.

Industry observers note that A model can also hallucinate and return different answers to the same input. A temperature of 0 makes varied answers less likely, but it doesn’t guarantee identical output. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails help you measure and contain these risks. A rule has neither problem, which is one reason regulated workloads favor rules. A useful test: If you can write the acceptance test as a rule, you can usually write the step as a rule. For more information, refer to Orchestration models: From rule-based to AI-native in AWS Prescriptive Guidance.

According to recent reports, most routing and classification steps sit between a rule and open-ended generation. A rule can’t decide every case, but these steps don’t need generated text either. They need one answer from a fixed list of options that you define in advance, like the support queues in the preceding example. Use a component that limits its output to the allowed answers and gives you a signal for when to escalate. Confident answers proceed, and uncertain ones escalate. The AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens describes this tiered, confidence-based escalation. On AWS, you can build it four ways:.

Recent findings suggest that the following JSON schema limits a structured-output answer to four queues plus ‘unsure’. Amazon Bedrock requires every object in the schema to set additionalProperties to false.

It has been revealed that whichever option you choose, check its escalation signal against your own labeled data, and set any threshold there. Keep your authorization decisions, such as a refund limit, in a rule.

Industry observers note that many cost patterns focus on routing between models. The fast path goes one level earlier: Run the deterministic check first, and send only what the rule can’t settle to a model. Intent routing is one example. Many messages carry an unambiguous signal, such as “refund” or “reset my password”, which a keyword match resolves in single-digit milliseconds or less. If rules resolve 95 percent of requests, only 1 in 20 requests reaches a model, before any savings from model selection. (Illustrative arithmetic, not a benchmark.).

On AWS, you compose this from existing building blocks:.

The following Choice state is a keyword fast path. It uses JSONata to send refund and password-reset messages straight to code, and it sends everything else to the constrained decision call.

You can also let a model write the rule once instead of running it every time. Have it draft a regular expression or a JSON schema, review it, and commit it. At runtime the rule runs at rule speed and cost. Review a model-written regular expression, and test it against known good and bad inputs. Avoid nested quantifiers such as (a+)+, which can make matching very slow on some inputs (regular expression denial of service, or ReDoS).

According to recent reports, when you do generate, Amazon Bedrock structured outputs constrain a response to a JSON schema that you define. The response then matches the schema, so your code can parse it without custom parsing logic (check content for correctness). Keep range checks, such as numeric bounds and length limits, in code. For supported models and schema features, refer to Get validated JSON results from models.

Recent findings suggest that if your rules live in configuration, allow only known primitives, such as regular expressions, schema checks, keyword lists, and range checks. Never run arbitrary code from a configuration file.

Recent findings suggest that choose the cheapest and fastest model that meets your quality floor. That is often not the newest or largest model. The Generative AI Lens covers this in its best practice on right-sizing model selection. Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock covers it in depth. Define the requirements before you compare models:.

Amazon Bedrock offers many model families and sizes behind one API, so you can right-size each task without changing your integration. Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing routes each request to a suitable model within a supported model family. Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation transfers knowledge from a larger model to a smaller, cheaper one for your use case. Model providers evaluate a upcoming frontier model on broad benchmarks, but your workload is one task with one quality floor. A larger model can add cost and latency without improving that task. Before you switch, evaluate each launch against your requirements, such as quality on your golden evaluation set and your latency target.

Sources indicate that the Generative AI Lens recommends testing candidate models against your ground truth data and having a way to update the model quickly. Go further and treat the decision as a tested configuration:.

Spend model capacity where judgment is needed, and nowhere else. You can get there in four steps:.

In this post, you learned how to decide whether a workflow step needs a model at all. Rules belong in deterministic code, and fixed choices belong in a constrained decision call. Open-ended work goes to a right-sized Amazon Bedrock model. Aim to meet each requirement at the lowest cost and latency that your quality floor allows. Ask whether a step needs a model before you ask which one.

For more information, refer to these posts on the AWS Artificial Intelligence Blog:.

To try a constrained decision call, open the Amazon Bedrock console, or deploy Strands Decider from its GitHub repository.

Start with one high-volume workflow and measure how much of it never needed a model.

Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super vital for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

Industry observers note that for each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

Recent findings suggest that on coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

According to recent reports, cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

An axiomatic foundation for optimized certainty equivalents

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (159 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22119v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Optimized Certainty Equivalents (OCEs) are an vital class of risk measures for optimization and risk management that includes the Mean--Variance criterion, Expected Shortfall, the Entropic Risk Measure, and expectation. Despite their importance, economic axioms have not characterized OCEs. We propose a new axiom called Fair-Coin Compensation, which characterizes OCEs together with Strong Risk Aversion and Normalization. We interpret Fair-Coin Compensation through the fair assignment of two losses by a coin toss: transfers between two participants can remove the additional risk created by the random assignment. Adding further axioms yields sharper characterizations. Monotonicity yields standard OCEs; Positive Homogeneity, together with Prudence, yields Expected Shortfall; and Fair-Coin Independence yields the Entropic Risk Measure. We also axiomatize the Mean--Variance criterion using our novel axiom of Equal-Mean Randomization, which states that random assignment of two losses with the same expected value does not produce a risk measure above the average of their risk measures.

CISA has added two fresh vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-97229 GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition Integer Overflow or Wraparound vulnerability CVE-2026-76418 Cisco Secure Firewall ASA Software and Cisco Secure FTD Software Unchecked Return Value to NULL Pointer Dereference Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not presently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.
